name: Aaron Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. I'll describe five pictures of the future and ask what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Northgate Fresh, a supermarket on the north side of town, and I start at five picking online orders. You get a handheld scanner, a trolley with six crates, and you race round the aisles filling people's orders before the vans leave at eight. After that I'm on the tills until one. I'm still not great at it, the picking supervisor Tasha says I pick too many bruised avocados.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what else is going on in your life?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the early start, the shop is quiet and it's like a puzzle. Outside work I fix up old bikes and sell them online, maybe three or four a month. Between the bikes, the early-shift premium and living with a flatmate, I've got well over six months saved and a few shares. I use AI every day, for pricing bikes, writing the adverts and working out repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough. The tools are handy but not magic, and I still use AI for my bike adverts. At work I'd say the picking app's route suggestions got a bit better and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a good world. The shop stays as it is, and the AI I already use keeps helping the bike side. I'd just carry on building both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the picking and till shifts and try to sell five or six bikes a month instead of three. I'd put some of my savings into a proper workshop space, maybe a shared unit near the station. I'd keep using AI for the listings and pricing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, quite upbeat. It's steady with room to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would the workshop cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shared unit near the station is about a month's wages a quarter. I'd only take it if the bikes paid for it within six months. If not, back to the shed at my mum's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see yourself at Northgate long term?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever, but for a few years, yes. It's steady money while the bike thing grows. I'd like to get better at picking, Tasha would be happy.

say: I'd say AI tools are **handy but not magic**.
I'd post that I still use AI for my **bike adverts**.
think: This is a **good world** for me, steady with room to grow.
AI keeps helping the **bike side** while the shop stays the same.
do: Sell **five or six bikes** a month instead of three.
Rent a **shared workshop** near the station if bikes cover it.
S0.quote: The tools are handy but not magic, and I still use AI for my bike adverts.
fieldNote: He already has a **side business** and uses AI daily for it.
He sets a clear **six-month test** before spending on a workshop.
The shop job is **steady money**, not his whole future.

steps.text: Raise bike sales to five or six a month
Rent the shared workshop unit near the station
Keep the dawn picking and till shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and it's better to get on with it. I'd tell people at work to learn the apps rather than fight them. Online I'd share how I use AI for small business stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks going to AI barely touch my shop work, but online picking is exactly what robots will do as they spread. My five o'clock picking shift is probably the first to go when robots spread into supermarkets. The bike business looks better and better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the bikes to a proper part-time business this year, register it and get the workshop. I'd ask Northgate if they need someone to help run the picking robots when they come. I'd move some savings from shares into tools and stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I've got a second leg to stand on, so I'm not nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Northgate would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev on the tills, who's 52 and only knows the till. Kev hates apps, he still writes the shift swaps on paper. I'd try to show Kev the basics, but you can't make someone want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you cut your Northgate hours to grow the bikes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd drop the till shift and keep the picking, because it's early and leaves the afternoons free. That's a pay cut, but my savings cover it. I'd check the numbers monthly.

I'd tell colleagues to **learn the apps** rather than fight them.

My **bike business** looks better and better.

Drop the **till shift** and move some savings into tools.
feel: **Calm**, with a second leg to stand on.

fieldNote: He sees his **picking shift** as the most exposed task.
A **side business** makes him calm where others would worry.

steps.text: Register the bike repair business and rent the workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is massive, and the government needs a plan for income, fast. I'm not a big politics guy, but this would be the exception. At work I'd tell people to save every penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's tight even for me. AGI by 2028 means AI can price, list and sell bikes better than me, and anyone can do it. Then robots by 2031 can fix bikes and pick orders. So my two legs both get kicked within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting money into the bike business and keep savings in cash. I'd use the three years before robots to do hands-on bike repair for people locally, because fixing someone's actual bike in person lasts longest. I'd learn whatever AI tools let one person run a repair shop cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the calm one, but this hits both my plans at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're adaptive and have savings. What's different this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Usually you adapt by moving to the next thing. Here the next thing is also going, a few years later. It's hard to adapt to a moving target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'm fine for a few years and not to worry. And I'd ask if I can use her shed again, so I'm not paying for the workshop. Save where you can.

say: I'd say the government needs an **income plan**, fast.
I'd tell colleagues at Northgate to **save every penny** while they still can.
think: AGI by 2028 means AI can **sell bikes** better than me.
Robots by 2031 kick **both my legs** within three years.
do: Stop investing in bikes and keep **savings in cash**.
Do **in-person repairs** locally during the three years before robots.
Move back to **mum's shed** to cut workshop costs.
feel: **Anxious**, unusual for me, because both plans get hit.
S2.quote: Usually you adapt by moving to the next thing. Here the next thing is also going, a few years later.
fieldNote: Being adaptive doesn't help when **every option** shrinks at once.
He shifts from growth to **cash and cost-cutting**.
He sees **in-person repair** as the longest-lasting work.

steps.text: Keep savings in cash instead of bike stock
Offer in-person bike repairs around the neighbourhood
Give up the workshop and use his mum's shed
Use AI tools to run repairs as a one-person shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives people time to get moving, so get moving. I'd share practical ideas online for small businesses. I'd still say the government should plan for income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my bike business has a good five years, and in-person repairs last until about 2034. That's long enough to make real money and save it. After that, I'd be 35 with savings, which is a decent place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the bike business hard for three years, use AI for everything that isn't hands-on, and save most of the profit. I'd leave Northgate in year two if the bikes pay enough. I'd keep an eye on what robots can actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a useful way. It's a race I think I can do well in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said save most of the profit. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For whatever comes after 2034, honestly I don't know what that is. Maybe it's money that keeps you going while everything shifts. I'd rather have it than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire anyone in the bike business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one person part time, Kev if he wanted it, actually. My old colleague Kev is good with his hands, just not with apps. That'd be a nice thing to do for a few years.

say: I'd say five years is time to **get moving**.
I'd still back a **government income plan** and share practical ideas for small businesses.
think: **In-person repairs** last until about 2034, long enough to make money.
At **35 with savings** I'd be in a decent place.
do: Grow the **bike business** hard for three years.
Leave Northgate in **year two** if bikes pay enough.
Save **most of the profit** for after 2034.
feel: **Uneasy** but useful, like a **race** I can do well in.
S3.quote: My old colleague Kev is good with his hands, just not with apps.
fieldNote: Five years turns his worry into a **race** he can win.
He plans to **bank profits** for an unknown future.

steps.text: Grow the bike repair business for three years
Leave Northgate once the bikes cover his costs
Save most of the bike profits
Use AI for pricing, adverts and bookings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so plan for it like any business would. I'd post about small business ideas and AI tools. I'd tell friends to use the decade well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I can build the bike shop properly and have it running for years before AGI. Robots for hands-on work come around 2039, when I'm 40. That's a lot of time to make and save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave Northgate within two years and open a small shop front for bikes. I'd use AI for the books, stock and adverts from day one. I'd also look at selling e-bikes and servicing them, since that's growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually excited. It's the version where I get to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that plan that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent on a shop front, mostly. If the high street is dying faster than the robots come, I'd be stuck with a lease. I'd sign short leases only.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would robots in 2039 end the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. Maybe I'd buy a robot and it'd fix bikes while I chat to customers. If I've built a name by then, people might still come to me. That's the bet.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, so plan like a business.
I'd post about **small business** ideas and AI tools.
think: I can build the bike shop and run it for **years before AGI**.
do: Leave Northgate and open a **bike shop front** within two years.
Use AI for **books, stock** and adverts from day one.
S4.quote: Maybe I'd buy a robot and it'd fix bikes while I chat to customers.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **own a business** rather than just survive.
He imagines **owning robots** rather than competing with them.

steps.text: Open a small bike shop on a short lease
Run the shop's books and stock with AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my job and my bikes both get hit before I've built anything. What would help is cheap small-business loans and some kind of income floor, so trying things isn't so risky. And clear dates on when shops plan to bring in robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about side hustles. Lots of people my age have one, and that changes how scary this all is. Nobody counts the second job when they talk about jobs disappearing.

headlineQuote: Nobody counts the second job when they talk about jobs disappearing.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** who picks online orders at dawn and works the tills at a supermarket.
He refurbishes and sells **bikes on the side**, and has over six months saved plus shares.
He uses AI daily and treats change as a **race** he can win with time.
He's calm in AI Plateau and Steady Disruption, **anxious** in AGI by 2028, calm again with ten years.
He'd leave the shop for his own **bike business** if the warning time allows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which hits his shop job and bike business together.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **small-business loans** and an income floor.
Clear dates on when shops bring in **robots**.
